questions.title: Why hypoglycemia is dangerous
questions.question: Why is hypoglycemia dangerous?

options.A: It affects the glucose supply to the brain

explanations.A: Correct. The brain relies almost entirely on a continuous supply of blood glucose (it cannot use fatty acids and only switches to ketone bodies after prolonged fasting), so hypoglycemia is dangerous specifically because it threatens that glucose supply -- producing neuroglycopenic symptoms such as confusion, seizures or coma if severe or prolonged. This is why prompt correction of hypoglycemia is a clinical priority, to protect ongoing cerebral glucose delivery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia is not itself irreversible; it is corrected by restoring blood glucose (via counter-regulatory hormones or glucose administration), though prolonged severe episodes can cause lasting brain injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucosuria requires hyperglycemia exceeding the renal threshold, the opposite of hypoglycemia's low blood glucose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypoglycemia does not produce hemolysis; that is unrelated to the danger being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that hypoglycemia is dangerous primarily because it threatens the brain's glucose supply.

field_notes.keySource: hand-drawn blue circle around option A, p1; fact-checked, no contradiction

questions.title: Complex I components
questions.question: In the electron transport chain, which of the following is not a component of Complex I?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is a component of Complex I). Complex I is built from roughly seven iron-sulfur centres that relay electrons toward coenzyme Q.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is a component of Complex I). Complex I is a large, multi-subunit assembly built from many polypeptides.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is a component of Complex I). NADH dehydrogenase (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is another name for Complex I itself, which accepts electrons from NADH.
explanations.D: Correct. Succinate dehydrogenase is a separate complex (Complex II) that accepts electrons from FADH2 generated in the TCA cycle -- it is not a component of Complex I, even though both ultimately feed electrons into the same respiratory chain. Recognising that succinate dehydrogenase is a separate complex is a common exam discriminator between the two respiratory-chain entry points.

questions.learning_objective: State that succinate dehydrogenase is not a component of Complex I, since it constitutes the separate Complex II.

questions.title: Glucosuria definition
questions.question: Which of the following is the best definition of Glucosuria?

options.B: It is the presence of detectable amount of glucose in urine
options.C: It is the presence of fructose and glucose in urine
options.D: It means presence of less than 25 mg/dl of glucose in urine

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucosuria is a urinary finding, not a synonym for diabetes mellitus -- diabetes mellitus is a disease that commonly causes glucosuria, but glucosuria itself is defined independently of that diagnosis.
explanations.B: Correct. Glucosuria is defined as the presence of a detectable amount of glucose in urine, occurring once plasma glucose filtered at the glomerulus exceeds the renal tubular reabsorptive capacity. This renal-threshold-based definition applies regardless of the underlying cause, whether diabetic or otherwise.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucosuria is defined by glucose in urine specifically, not a combination with fructose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucosuria is not bounded by a specific low threshold such as "less than 25 mg/dl" -- it is simply detectable glucose in urine, at levels that in practice are well above such a low figure once the renal threshold is exceeded.

questions.learning_objective: Define glucosuria as detectable glucose in the urine, distinguishing it from diabetes mellitus.

field_notes.keySource: hand-drawn blue circle around option B, p15; fact-checked, no contradiction

questions.title: Hypoglycemia's blood glucose threshold
questions.question: Mr Akmal was diagnosed to have hypoglycemia. Which of the following blood glucose levels reveals it?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 60 mg/dl is above this course's hypoglycemic threshold, sitting in a borderline range rather than confirming hypoglycemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 80 mg/dl is within the normal fasting glucose range, not a hypoglycemic value.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Less than 100 mg/dl" is too broad and includes most of the normal fasting range; it does not specifically confirm hypoglycemia.
explanations.D: Correct. This course's working definition diagnoses hypoglycemia at a blood glucose level below 45 mg/dl, the lowest and most specific of the options offered. Recognising this course's specific numeric cutoff, rather than a higher or vaguer figure, is what the question is testing.

questions.learning_objective: State that this course defines hypoglycemia as a blood glucose level below 45 mg/dl.

field_notes.keySource: hand-drawn blue circle around option D, p13; fact-checked, no contradiction (course-specific cutoff, see concept uncertainty note)

questions.title: TCA enzyme that is also an ETC member
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes of the TCA cycle is a member of the electron transport chain?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyses a TCA-cycle oxidation step but is a soluble mitochondrial matrix enzyme, not embedded in the inner membrane as an ETC complex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase catalyses a TCA-cycle oxidation step but, like isocitrate dehydrogenase, is a matrix enzyme, not an ETC complex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Succinate thiokinase (succinyl-CoA synthetase) generates GTP/ATP in the TCA cycle via substrate-level phosphorylation, but is not part of the electron transport chain.
explanations.D: Correct. Succinate dehydrogenase is unique among TCA-cycle enzymes in being embedded directly in the inner mitochondrial membrane and doubling as Complex II of the electron transport chain, oxidising succinate to fumarate while passing electrons (via FAD) into the chain at coenzyme Q. No other TCA enzyme sits directly in the inner mitochondrial membrane as part of a respiratory complex the way succinate dehydrogenase does.

questions.learning_objective: Identify succinate dehydrogenase as the TCA-cycle enzyme that also functions as ETC Complex II.

questions.title: Hormone that is NOT anti-insulin
questions.question: Which of the following hormones is not anti-insulin?

explanations.A: Correct. Parathormone (PTH) regulates plasma calcium and phosphate (via bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption and vitamin D activation), not glucose homeostasis -- it has no anti-insulin (counter-regulatory) role, unlike the other three options. Keeping the glucose-regulating and calcium-regulating hormone families separate avoids misattributing parathormone's effects to blood glucose control.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is anti-insulin). Adrenaline is a genuine counter-regulatory hormone, raising blood glucose via glycogenolysis, opposing insulin's effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is anti-insulin). Growth hormone genuinely is anti-insulin: it reduces peripheral glucose uptake and promotes lipolysis, raising blood glucose over time.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this is anti-insulin). Glucagon is a genuine counter-regulatory hormone, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to raise blood glucose, directly opposing insulin.

questions.learning_objective: State that parathormone is not an anti-insulin hormone, distinguishing its calcium-regulating role from the glucose-raising role of adrenaline, growth hormone and glucagon.
